summary.text: For each prime \(p\), counting pairs divisible by \(p^i\) and applying the factorial valuation formula expresses the quotient’s \(p\)-adic valuation as \(\sum_{i\ge1}\bigl(M_i^2-\sum_{k=1}^{M_i}k\lfloor M_i/k\rfloor\bigr)\), where \(M_i=\lfloor n/p^i\rfloor\). Each summand is nonnegative and is positive exactly when \(M_i\ge3\); hence the total is positive exactly when \(M_1\ge3\), equivalently \(p\le\lfloor n/3\rfloor\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N(n)=\prod_{j=1}^{n}\prod_{k=1}^{n}\gcd(j,k),
\qquad
D(n)=\prod_{k=1}^{n}\left(\left\lfloor\frac nk\right\rfloor!\right)^k.
\]
Thus the sequence term in the statement is
\[
a(n)=\frac{N(n)}{D(n)},
\]
where the quotient is taken in the natural numbers. We will first prove that this division is exact, and then determine when a given prime divides the quotient.

For a prime \(q\), write \(v_q(m)\) for the exponent of \(q\) in the prime factorization of a positive integer \(m\). We shall compute the \(q\)-adic valuations of both \(N(n)\) and \(D(n)\).

For clarity, whenever a sum is written as \(\sum_{i\ge 1}\), it is in fact finite: all its terms vanish once \(q^i>n\).

First consider the numerator. For positive integers \(j,k\),
\[
v_q(\gcd(j,k))=\min(v_q(j),v_q(k)).
\]
Also,
\[
\min(v_q(j),v_q(k))
 =\sum_{i\ge1}\mathbf 1_{q^i\mid j\,\text{ and }\,q^i\mid k},
\]
because the summand is \(1\) precisely for \(i=1,\ldots,\min(v_q(j),v_q(k))\). Therefore, using additivity of valuations on products and interchanging finite sums,
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_q(N(n))
&=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}v_q(\gcd(j,k))\\
&=\sum_{i\ge1}
  \#\{1\le j\le n:q^i\mid j\}
  \#\{1\le k\le n:q^i\mid k\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
There are exactly \(\lfloor n/q^i\rfloor\) multiples of \(q^i\) between \(1\) and \(n\). Hence
\[
\boxed{
 v_q(N(n))=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2.}
\tag{1}
\]

Now consider the denominator. Legendre's formula says that for every nonnegative integer \(m\),
\[
v_q(m!)=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Indeed, for each \(i\), the term \(\lfloor m/q^i\rfloor\) counts the factors among \(1,\ldots,m\) which contribute at least an \(i\)-th factor of \(q\). Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_q(D(n))
&=\sum_{k=1}^{n} k\,v_q\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac nk\right\rfloor!\right)\\
&=\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\sum_{i\ge1}
  \left\lfloor
  \frac{\lfloor n/k\rfloor}{q^i}
  \right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
Successive integer division satisfies
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor n/k\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac{n}{kq^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Consequently, after interchanging the finite sums,
\[
\boxed{
 v_q(D(n))
 =\sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{k=1}^{n}
 k\left\lfloor\frac{n}{kq^i}\right\rfloor.}
\tag{2}
\]

We next analyze the inner sum in (2). Define, for every nonnegative integer \(M\),
\[
S(M)=\sum_{k=1}^{M}k\left\lfloor\frac Mk\right\rfloor.
\]
Fix \(i\ge1\) and put
\[
M_i=\left\lfloor\frac{n}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Again using the rule for successive integer divisions,
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{n}{kq^i}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor n/q^i\rfloor}{k}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac{M_i}{k}\right\rfloor.
\]
If \(k>M_i\), this last quotient is zero. Therefore
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\left\lfloor\frac{n}{kq^i}\right\rfloor
=\sum_{k=1}^{M_i}k\left\lfloor\frac{M_i}{k}\right\rfloor
=S(M_i).
\]
Thus (2) becomes
\[
\boxed{v_q(D(n))=\sum_{i\ge1}S(M_i),}
\qquad
\boxed{v_q(N(n))=\sum_{i\ge1}M_i^2.}
\tag{3}
\]

The decisive elementary estimate is
\[
S(M)\le M^2
\tag{4}
\]
for every \(M\ge0\), with equality exactly when \(M\le2\).

To prove the weak inequality, observe that for each \(1\le k\le M\),
\[
k\left\lfloor\frac Mk\right\rfloor\le M.
\]
There are \(M\) summands, so their sum is at most \(M\cdot M=M^2\).

For \(M=0,1,2\), direct evaluation gives
\[
S(0)=0,
\qquad
S(1)=1,
\qquad
S(2)=1\cdot2+2\cdot1=4,
\]
so equality holds in these three cases.

Suppose now that \(M\ge3\). The summand with \(k=M-1\) is strictly smaller than \(M\). Indeed,
\[
M-1\le M<2(M-1),
\]
so
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{M}{M-1}\right\rfloor=1

equalspace
\text{and hence}

equalspace
(M-1)\left\lfloor\frac{M}{M-1}\right\rfloor=M-1<M.
\]
Every other summand is at most \(M\), as above. Therefore the sum of all \(M\) summands is strictly less than \(M^2\). We have proved
\[
\boxed{
S(M)=M^2\ \text{if }M\le2,
\qquad
S(M)<M^2\ \text{if }M\ge3.}
\tag{5}
\]

We can now establish the exactness of the quotient defining \(a(n)\). From (3) and (4), for every prime \(q\),
\[
v_q(D(n))=\sum_{i\ge1}S(M_i)
\le \sum_{i\ge1}M_i^2
=v_q(N(n)).
\]
Both \(N(n)\) and \(D(n)\) are positive: every gcd occurring in \(N(n)\) is positive, and every factorial and its powers occurring in \(D(n)\) are positive. By unique prime factorization, a positive integer divides another positive integer exactly when its valuation at every prime is no larger. Hence
\[
D(n)\mid N(n).
\]
Thus \(a(n)=N(n)/D(n)\) is an exact positive integer, and for every prime \(p\),
\[
v_p(a(n))=v_p(N(n))-v_p(D(n)).
\tag{6}
\]

We now fix the prime \(p\) from the statement. Set
\[
M_i=\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Equations (3) and (6) give
\[
v_p(a(n))
=\sum_{i\ge1}\bigl(M_i^2-S(M_i)\bigr).
\tag{7}
\]
Every summand on the right is nonnegative by (4). By (5), such a summand is zero exactly when \(M_i\le2\), and it is positive exactly when \(M_i\ge3\).

Because \(p\ge2\), the powers \(p^i\) increase with \(i\), and hence
\[
M_i=\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^i}\right\rfloor
\le \left\lfloor\frac np\right\rfloor=M_1
\qquad(i\ge1).
\]
It follows that all summands in (7) vanish exactly when \(M_1\le2\). Conversely, if \(M_1\ge3\), then the summand for \(i=1\) is already strictly positive, while all other summands are nonnegative. Therefore
\[
\boxed{
v_p(a(n))>0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\left\lfloor\frac np\right\rfloor\ge3.}
\tag{8}
\]

For completeness, this is also the two relevant cases explicitly.

If \(p>\lfloor n/3\rfloor\), then \(n<3p\). Hence \(\lfloor n/p\rfloor<3\), so \(M_1\le2\). Since every \(M_i\le M_1\), formula (5) gives \(S(M_i)=M_i^2\) for every \(i\). Thus the valuations of numerator and denominator are equal and \(v_p(a(n))=0\).

If \(p\le\lfloor n/3\rfloor\), then \(3p\le n\). Therefore \(\lfloor n/p\rfloor\ge3\). At \(i=1\), formula (5) gives
\[
S\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac np\right\rfloor\right)
<\left\lfloor\frac np\right\rfloor^2.
\]
For every other \(i\), the corresponding denominator contribution is at most the numerator contribution. Summing, we obtain
\[
v_p(D(n))<v_p(N(n)),
\]
and consequently \(v_p(a(n))>0\).

Finally, because \(a(n)>0\), a prime \(p\) divides \(a(n)\) exactly when \(v_p(a(n))>0\). Also, for positive \(p\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac np\right\rfloor\ge3
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
3p\le n
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p\le\left\lfloor\frac n3\right\rfloor.
\]
Combining this equivalence with (8) yields
\[
\boxed{
p\mid a(n)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p\le\left\lfloor\frac n3\right\rfloor.}
\]
This proves the conjecture for every positive integer \(n\) and every prime \(p\).
